3.1 Conditional doubling
Start with four independent finite-energy  $m$ -mode input systems in the state
$\rho_{A_{1}}\otimes\rho_{B_{1}}\otimes\rho_{A_{2}}\otimes\rho_{B_{2}}.$
(24)
The two pairs may be different. Mix  $A_{1},A_{2}$  on a balanced beam splitter,
and independently mix  $B_{1},B_{2}$  in the same way:
$R_{A_{+}}=\frac{R_{A_{1}}+R_{A_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad R_{A_{-}}=\frac{-R_{A_{1}}+R_{A_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}},$
(25)
with analogous definitions for  $B$ . We call these two balanced
beam splitters the copy step. Then apply the  $\eta$ -beam splitter
$U_{\eta}$  to  $A_{+}B_{+}$  and to  $A_{-}B_{-}$ , producing  $C_{+}E_{+}$  and  $C_{-}E_{-}$ .
Set  $M=A_{+}B_{+}$  before converting it unitarily to  $C_{+}E_{+}$ .
To specify the states underlying these labels, write  $\zeta$  for the state
after the copy step:
$\displaystyle\zeta_{A_{+}A_{-}B_{+}B_{-}}={}$
$\displaystyle\bigl[U_{1/2}(\rho_{A_{1}}\otimes\rho_{A_{2}})U_{1/2}^{\dagger}\bigr]\otimes\bigl[U_{1/2}(\rho_{B_{1}}\otimes\rho_{B_{2}})U_{1/2}^{\dagger}\bigr].$
(26)
Tensor factors are reordered according to their labels. Applying
$\mathcal{B}_{\eta}$  to the minus pair and retaining  $M$  gives a state on  $C_{-}M$ .
Applying the  $\eta$ -beam splitter to  $M$  then gives the same state on
$C_{-}C_{+}E_{+}$ .
The latter is a marginal of the four-output state, denoted
$\Xi_{C_{+}E_{+}C_{-}E_{-}}$ . The labels  $M$  and  $C_{+}E_{+}$  describe the
memory before and after its  $\eta$ -beam splitter, respectively.
This construction is a quantum version of the doubling trick used in
classical Gaussian extremality arguments [15]. Here the
conditional qEPI provides the nonnegative remainder. Mixing two input pairs separates
their total deficit into the deficit of the plus pair, the deficit of
the minus pair conditioned on the plus inputs, and a correlation term.
The following identity makes all three terms nonnegative. Allowing the two input pairs to differ will let us
choose a thermal auxiliary in Section 3.4.
Lemma 3 (Doubling with different pairs).
Let  $\zeta_{A_{-}B_{-}M}$  be the state in (26), with tensor factors
reordered and  $M=A_{+}B_{+}$ . Define
$\zeta_{C_{-}M}=(\mathcal{B}_{\eta}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{M})(\zeta_{A_{-}B_{-}M}).$
The conditional deficit below uses these two states; the CMI is evaluated
in the four-output state  $\Xi$ . For each fixed  $p\in[0,1]$ ,
$\displaystyle F_{p}(A_{1},B_{1})+F_{p}(A_{2},B_{2})=F_{p}(A_{+},B_{+})+F_{p}(A_{-},B_{-}\mid M)+I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+}).$
(27)
All three terms on the right are nonnegative.
Proof.
The product in (26) proves independence between the entire
$A$ -group and the entire  $B$ -group. Indeed,
$\displaystyle S(A_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})=S(A_{-}A_{+})+S(B_{+})-S(A_{+})-S(B_{+})=S(A_{-}\mid A_{+}).$
(28)
Similarly  $S(B_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})=S(B_{-}\mid B_{+})$ . Moreover
$S(A_{-}B_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})=S(A_{-}\mid A_{+})+S(B_{-}\mid B_{+}),$
(29)
which verifies conditional independence explicitly. Hence
$\displaystyle I(A_{-};B_{-}\mid A_{+}B_{+})$
$\displaystyle=0,$
$\displaystyle S(A_{-}\mid M)$
$\displaystyle=S(A_{-}\mid A_{+}),$
$\displaystyle S(B_{-}\mid M)$
$\displaystyle=S(B_{-}\mid B_{+}).$
(30)
The  $A$  entropy terms in the right side of (27) satisfy
$\displaystyle S(A_{+})+S(A_{-}\mid M)$
$\displaystyle=S(A_{+}A_{-})$
$\displaystyle=S(A_{1}A_{2})=S(A_{1})+S(A_{2}),$
(31)
where the final equality uses independence of the original inputs.
Multiplication by  $-p$  gives the desired  $A$  contribution; the  $B$  argument
is identical with coefficient  $-(1-p)$ .
The output terms combine as
$\displaystyle S(C_{+})+S(C_{-}\mid M)+I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})$
$\displaystyle\qquad=S(C_{+})+S(C_{-}\mid C_{+})$
$\displaystyle\qquad=S(C_{+}C_{-}).$
(32)
The equality of the two conditional entropies follows by applying the
$\eta$ -beam splitter to the memory in both entropy terms:
$\displaystyle S(C_{-}\mid M)_{\zeta}$
$\displaystyle=S(C_{-}M)_{\zeta}-S(M)_{\zeta}$
$\displaystyle=S(C_{-}C_{+}E_{+})_{\Xi}-S(C_{+}E_{+})_{\Xi}$
$\displaystyle=S(C_{-}\mid C_{+}E_{+})_{\Xi}.$
(33)
The copy step commutes with the  $\eta$ -beam splitters: the former
acts on the pair index and the latter on the  $A/B$  index. To check this directly, put
$a=\sqrt{\eta}$ ,  $b=\sqrt{1-\eta}$  and first define
$R_{C_{i}}=aR_{A_{i}}+bR_{B_{i}}$  and
$R_{E_{i}}=-bR_{A_{i}}+aR_{B_{i}}$  for  $i=1,2$ . Substitution shows
$R_{C_{+}}=\frac{R_{C_{1}}+R_{C_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad R_{C_{-}}=\frac{-R_{C_{1}}+R_{C_{2}}}{\sqrt{2}},$
(34)
with the same identities for  $E_{+},E_{-}$ . Both circuit orderings therefore
have the same action on all Weyl operators and the same joint output state.
If the  $\eta$ -beam splitters act first,
$C_{1},C_{2}$  are independent and the copy step acts unitarily on them.
Therefore  $S(C_{+}C_{-})=S(C_{1})+S(C_{2})$ . The two constant terms on the right
are  $2m\,d(p\|\eta)$ , proving the identity.
Since all initial energies are finite and passive beam splitters
preserve total energy, every joint entropy here is finite. The first term is nonnegative by unconditional affine qEPI, the second by
conditional affine qEPI and (30), and the third by strong
subadditivity. ∎
The consequence needed for linear equality is obtained by setting  $p=\eta$ :
$\displaystyle L_{\eta}(A_{1},B_{1})=L_{\eta}(A_{2},B_{2})=0$
(35)
$\displaystyle{}\Longrightarrow I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})=0.$
3.2 A thermal channel with a common vacuum component
For  $N>0$ , define the  $m$ -mode product thermal state with mean photon number
$N$  per mode by
$\tau_{N}=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{m}\left[\frac{1}{N+1}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{N}{N+1}\right)^{n}|n\rangle\!\langle n|\right].$
(36)
Set  $\tau_{0}=|0\rangle\!\langle 0|$  when  $N=0$ . Its covariance is  $(N+\frac{1}{2})I_{2m}$ .
Fix once and for all the channel
$\Phi(\rho)=\mathcal{B}_{1/2}(\rho\otimes\tau_{2}).$
(37)
This is the thermal attenuator of transmissivity  $1/2$  with
environment  $\tau_{2}$ . The environment energy  $N=2$  makes it a
measure-and-prepare channel: a heterodyne measurement followed by
preparation of a displaced  $\tau_{1/2}$  state. Such a
channel is entanglement breaking: when applied to one part of a joint
state, its output is a mixture of product states. We use the more specific
fact that every prepared state contains a component along the vacuum.
Any bath mean photon number  $N>1$  gives a similar representation,
with prepared thermal mean  $(N-1)/2>0$ . The choice  $N=2$  keeps the
constants simple. The transmissivity of  $\Phi$  is  $1/2$ , independent
of the physical  $\eta$ .
3.2.1 Measure-and-prepare representation
For  $z\in\mathbb{C}^{m}$ , the coherent state is
$|z\rangle=\mathcal{D}(z)|0\rangle=e^{-|z|^{2}/2}\sum_{\bm{n}\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{m}}\frac{z_{1}^{n_{1}}\cdots z_{m}^{n_{m}}}{\sqrt{n_{1}!\cdots n_{m}!}}|\bm{n}\rangle.$
(38)
It satisfies
$\langle u|v\rangle=\exp[-(|u|^{2}+|v|^{2})/2+\bar{u}\cdot v]$ .
The heterodyne measurement is the positive-operator-valued measure
(POVM)
$M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z)=\pi^{-m}|z\rangle\langle z|\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z)=I.$
(39)
A POVM assigns positive operators to measurable outcome sets and sums to
the identity;  $\mathrm{d}^{2m}z$  denotes Lebesgue measure in the real and imaginary
coordinates of  $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ . The second identity in (39) follows
by inserting (38) and integrating its number-basis entries.
For a state  $\rho$ , the outcome density is its Husimi
$Q$ -function [28],
$Q_{\rho}(z)=\pi^{-m}\langle z|\rho|z\rangle,\qquad\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}Q_{\rho}(z)\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z=1.$
(40)
Holevo [29, Theorem 2, Eqs. (30)–(31)] gives the
general measure-and-prepare form of entanglement-breaking Gaussian
channels. The representation below is the special case for  $\Phi$ ; the
direct verification fixes the environment photon number and the
prepared-state noise in our convention.
Lemma 4.
For every input state,
$\displaystyle\Phi(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}Q_{\rho}(z)\,\pi_{z}\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z,$
$\displaystyle\pi_{z}$
$\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}(z/\sqrt{2})\tau_{1/2}\mathcal{D}(z/\sqrt{2})^{\dagger}.$
(41)
Proof.
Use the complex displacement characteristic function
$\widehat{\rho}(w)=\operatorname{Tr}\rho\mathcal{D}(w)$ . The heterodyne Fourier identity is
$\int Q_{\rho}(z)e^{\sum_{j}(w_{j}\bar{z}_{j}-\bar{w}_{j}z_{j})}\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z=\widehat{\rho}(w)e^{-|w|^{2}/2}.$
(42)
The thermal characteristic function is
$\widehat{\tau_{N}}(w)=e^{-(N+1/2)|w|^{2}},$
as follows from its Gaussian covariance  $(N+1/2)I$  and
(16). For a displaced state,
$\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{D}(\alpha)\rho\mathcal{D}(\alpha)^{\dagger}\mathcal{D}(w)]=e^{w\cdot\bar{\alpha}-\bar{w}\cdot\alpha}\widehat{\rho}(w).$
Let  $\Phi_{\rm prep}$  denote the integral map on the right of (41).
The three factors in its characteristic function are
$\displaystyle\widehat{\Phi_{\rm prep}(\rho)}(w)$
$\displaystyle=e^{-|w|^{2}}\int Q_{\rho}(z)e^{(w\cdot\bar{z}-\bar{w}\cdot z)/\sqrt{2}}\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{=}e^{-|w|^{2}}\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-|w|^{2}/4}$
$\displaystyle=\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-5|w|^{2}/4}.$
(43)
Step (a) uses the Fourier identity (42) at  $w/\sqrt{2}$ ;
Appendix A.3 gives its coherent-state verification.
On the other hand, the beam-splitter formula gives
$\widehat{\Phi(\rho)}(w)=\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})\widehat{\tau_{2}}(w/\sqrt{2})=\widehat{\rho}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-5|w|^{2}/4}.$
(44)
Uniqueness of characteristic functions proves (41).
The integral is in trace norm; its justification is in
Appendix A.
∎
3.2.2 The vacuum component
Lemma 5.
Each state in (41) satisfies
$\pi_{z}\geq c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|,\qquad c(z)=\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)^{m}e^{-|z|^{2}}\in(0,1).$
(45)
Thus  $\pi_{z}=c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|+(1-c(z))\kappa_{z}$  for a measurable family of states
$\kappa_{z}$ .
Proof.
The thermal formula gives  $\tau_{1/2}=(2/3)^{m}3^{-H_{m}}$ . With
$\alpha=z/\sqrt{2}$ ,
$\displaystyle\langle 0|\pi_{z}^{-1}|0\rangle$
$\displaystyle=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{m}\langle-\alpha|3^{H_{m}}|-\alpha\rangle$
$\displaystyle=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{m}e^{2|\alpha|^{2}}=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^{m}e^{|z|^{2}}.$
(46)
For one mode the required series is
$\langle\alpha|3^{a^{\dagger}a}|\alpha\rangle=e^{-|\alpha|^{2}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{3^{n}|\alpha|^{2n}}{n!}=e^{2|\alpha|^{2}};$
(47)
multiplication over the modes proves the middle equality of
(46). Each prepared thermal state has zero kernel. The inverse in that equation is interpreted as its
quadratic form, namely  $\left\lVert\pi_{z}^{-1/2}|0\rangle\right\rVert^{2}$ .
In particular  $\pi_{z}^{-1/2}|0\rangle$  is a well-defined Hilbert
space vector. For every vector  $v$ , Cauchy–Schwarz gives
$|\langle 0|v\rangle|^{2}=|\langle\pi_{z}^{-1/2}0,\pi_{z}^{1/2}v\rangle|^{2}\leq\langle 0|\pi_{z}^{-1}|0\rangle\,\langle v,\pi_{z}v\rangle.$
(48)
This is the operator inequality (45) with the reciprocal
of (46). Define
$\kappa_{z}=(\pi_{z}-c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|)/(1-c(z))$ . It is positive and has trace
one. The map  $z\mapsto\pi_{z}$  is trace-norm continuous, as follows from
strong continuity of displacements acting on a trace-class operator.
The function  $c(z)$  is continuous and  $1-c(z)\geq 1-(2/3)^{m}>0$ .
Thus  $z\mapsto\kappa_{z}$  is trace-norm continuous, in particular measurable.
∎
3.3 A two-outcome instrument and strict information loss
The vacuum component in Lemma 5 allows us to split  $\Phi$
into two branches. In one branch the channel prepares the vacuum and
therefore discards all correlations with a reference system. We shall
show that this branch has positive probability for every input and that
its preceding filter cannot turn a correlated state into a product.
These two facts give the required equality criterion.
Integrating the vacuum weight against the heterodyne POVM defines the
effect (a positive operator bounded by the identity)
$G=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}c(z)M_{\rm het}(\mathrm{d}z)=3^{-m}2^{-H_{m}},\qquad 0<G\leq 3^{-m}I.$
(49)
Here  $0<G$  means that  $G$  has zero kernel, not that it has a positive
uniform lower bound. To check the formula, in one mode insert the
coherent-state expansion and integrate in polar coordinates:
$\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}e^{-|z|^{2}}|z\rangle\langle z|\,\mathrm{d}^{2}z=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-(n+1)}|n\rangle\langle n|.$
(50)
Multiplication over the modes and the factor  $(2/3)^{m}$  in  $c(z)$  give
(49).
Equation (50) is the Glauber–Sudarshan
$P$ -representation of the thermal state with one photon per
mode [30]; thus  $G=(2/3)^{m}\tau_{1}$  is a multiple of a thermal
state.
Define two completely positive maps by
$\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}(G\rho)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|,$
$\displaystyle\Lambda_{0}(\rho)$
$\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{C}^{m}}Q_{\rho}(z)[\pi_{z}-c(z)|0\rangle\!\langle 0|]\,\mathrm{d}^{2m}z.$
(51)
The kernel in the second integral is positive by
Lemma 5; hence it defines a completely positive
measure-and-prepare map. Its trace is
$\operatorname{Tr}\Lambda_{0}(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}[(I-G)\rho]$ , and
$\Phi=\Lambda_{1}+\Lambda_{0}$ . Complete positivity of the integral maps is verified in
Appendix A.4.
For  $f=0,1$ , let
$M_{1}=G^{1/2},\qquad M_{0}=(I-G)^{1/2},\qquad\mathcal{I}_{f}(\rho)=M_{f}\rho M_{f}.$
(52)
Since  $M_{0}^{2}+M_{1}^{2}=I$ , the map
$\mathcal{M}(\rho)=\sum_{f=0}^{1}|f\rangle\langle f|_{F}\otimes\mathcal{I}_{f}(\rho)$
(53)
is a channel. It records a two-valued outcome in the classical register
$F$  and retains the filtered input, denoted  $X^{\prime}$ . Moreover,
$I-G\geq(1-3^{-m})I$ , so  $(I-G)^{-1/2}$  is bounded and
$\Psi_{0}(\sigma)=\Lambda_{0}\bigl((I-G)^{-1/2}\sigma(I-G)^{-1/2}\bigr)$
(54)
is a channel: it is completely positive, and its trace is  $\operatorname{Tr}\sigma$ .
After the instrument, replace  $X^{\prime}$  by the vacuum when  $F=1$  and apply
$\Psi_{0}$  when  $F=0$ . Discarding  $F$  then gives exactly  $\Phi$ , since
$\Psi_{0}\circ\mathcal{I}_{0}=\Lambda_{0}$ .
Proposition 6 (Strict information loss for  $\Phi$ ).
Let  $\omega_{XK}$  be a state such that  $X$  consists of  $m\geq 1$  bosonic
modes with  $\operatorname{Tr}(\omega_{X}H_{m})<\infty$ , and the reference system  $K$  has a
separable Hilbert space with  $S(\omega_{K})<\infty$ . Write
$\zeta_{YK}=(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K})(\omega_{XK})$ . Then
$I(X;K)_{\omega}=I(Y;K)_{\zeta}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\omega_{XK}=\omega_{X}\otimes\omega_{K}.$
(55)
Proof.
Let  $p_{f}=\operatorname{Tr}(M_{f}\omega_{X}M_{f})$ . Equation (49)
implies  $p_{1}>0$ , because all its number-basis eigenvalues are positive,
and  $p_{0}\geq 1-3^{-m}>0$ . The conditional states after the instrument are
$\omega^{f}_{X^{\prime}K}=p_{f}^{-1}(M_{f}\otimes I_{K})\omega_{XK}(M_{f}\otimes I_{K}).$
(56)
Let  $\zeta^{0}_{YK}=(\Psi_{0}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K})(\omega^{0}_{X^{\prime}K})$  and
$\zeta^{1}_{YK}=|0\rangle\!\langle 0|_{Y}\otimes\omega_{K}^{1}$ . Both transformations preserve
the corresponding  $K$  marginal. The state with the flag retained is
$\zeta_{FYK}=\sum_{f}p_{f}|f\rangle\langle f|_{F}\otimes\zeta^{f}_{YK}$ .
All branch and joint entropies below are finite, as verified in
Appendix A.4. Thus ordinary entropy chain rules apply.
Data processing for  $\mathcal{M}$ , followed by the chain rule for a
classical flag, gives
$\displaystyle I(X;K)_{\omega}$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\geq}I(FX^{\prime};K)_{(\mathcal{M}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{K})(\omega)}$
$\displaystyle=I(F;K)+p_{1}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{1}}+p_{0}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{0}}.$
(57)
On the other hand, discarding the flag and then using data processing
for  $\Psi_{0}$  gives
$\displaystyle I(Y;K)_{\zeta}$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\leq}I(FY;K)_{\zeta}$
$\displaystyle=I(F;K)+p_{0}I(Y;K)_{\zeta^{0}}$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(c)}}{\leq}I(F;K)+p_{0}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{0}}.$
(58)
Steps (a), (b), and (c) apply data processing to the instrument,
discarding the flag, and the channel  $\Psi_{0}$ , respectively.
The  $FK$  marginal is the same in both displays, and the  $f=1$  term
vanishes in the second display because  $\zeta^{1}$  is a product.
Subtracting yields
$I(X;K)_{\omega}-I(Y;K)_{\zeta}\geq p_{1}I(X^{\prime};K)_{\omega^{1}}.$
(59)
If the left side is zero, then  $\omega^{1}=\omega^{1}_{X^{\prime}}\otimes\omega^{1}_{K}$ .
Taking its  $X^{\prime}$  marginal in (56) therefore gives
$(G^{1/2}\otimes I_{K})\omega_{XK}(G^{1/2}\otimes I_{K})=(G^{1/2}\omega_{X}G^{1/2})\otimes\omega_{K}^{1}.$
(60)
For number-basis vectors  $|\bm{n}\rangle,|\bm{n}^{\prime}\rangle$ , their eigenvalues
$g_{\bm{n}}=3^{-m}2^{-\sum_{j}n_{j}}$  and  $g_{\bm{n}^{\prime}}$  are positive.
Taking the corresponding operator block of (60)
and cancelling  $\sqrt{g_{\bm{n}}g_{\bm{n}^{\prime}}}$  gives
$\langle\bm{n}|\omega_{XK}|\bm{n}^{\prime}\rangle=\langle\bm{n}|\omega_{X}|\bm{n}^{\prime}\rangle\,\omega_{K}^{1}.$
Equality of all blocks implies  $\omega_{XK}=\omega_{X}\otimes\omega_{K}^{1}$ .
Taking the partial trace over  $X$  identifies  $\omega_{K}^{1}=\omega_{K}$ .
The converse holds because a local channel preserves product states.
∎
Remark 7.
The filter  $G^{1/2}$  is injective, although its inverse is unbounded.
The number-basis argument above uses only its positive eigenvalues;
it does not apply the inverse to a trace-class operator. This distinction
is useful when seeking quantitative versions of (59).
We also note why the standard equality condition for data
processing does not suffice here. By Petz’s theorem [31, 32],
equality in (55) implies that  $\omega_{XK}$  is
recovered from  $\zeta_{YK}$  by a local channel on  $Y$ ; since  $\Phi$  is
entanglement breaking, this only shows that  $\omega_{XK}$  is separable,
whereas the instrument argument yields a product.
3.4 From equality to independent outputs
Proof of (i) $\Rightarrow$ (ii) in Theorem 1.
Let  $\omega_{CE}=U_{\eta}(\rho_{A}\otimes\rho_{B})U_{\eta}^{\dagger}$  and assume
$L_{\eta}(A,B)=0$ .
1. Add a thermal equality pair.
In Lemma 3, set
$(\rho_{A_{1}},\rho_{B_{1}})=(\rho_{A},\rho_{B}),\qquad(\rho_{A_{2}},\rho_{B_{2}})=(\tau_{2},\tau_{2}).$
(61)
All four inputs are independent. If the original energies are  $\mathsf{E}_{A},\mathsf{E}_{B}$ ,
the total energy in this circuit is  $\mathsf{E}_{A}+\mathsf{E}_{B}+4m$ . Every beam splitter preserves
that total, so the energy bound (9) makes all circuit entropies finite.
The auxiliary state has the form
$(\tau_{2})_{A_{2}}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{B_{2}}=3^{-2m}\exp[-\log(3/2)(H_{A_{2}}+H_{B_{2}})].$
Since  $U_{\eta}$  preserves  $H_{A_{2}}+H_{B_{2}}$ , it preserves this state:
$U_{\eta}(\tau_{2}\otimes\tau_{2})U_{\eta}^{\dagger}=(\tau_{2})_{G_{C}}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{E}}.$
(62)
In particular, the auxiliary outputs are independent and
$L_{\eta}(A_{2},B_{2})=mg(2)-\eta mg(2)-(1-\eta)mg(2)=0$ .
2. Apply the doubling identity.
Use the first circuit order in Fig. 1(a), with
$M=A_{+}B_{+}$ . Lemma 3, at  $p=\eta$ , gives
$0=L_{\eta}(A_{+},B_{+})+L_{\eta}(A_{-},B_{-}\mid M)+I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})_{\Xi}.$
(63)
The lemma verifies the conditional-independence hypothesis needed for
the conditional deficit. All three terms are nonnegative, hence
$I(C_{-};E_{+}\mid C_{+})_{\Xi}=0.$
(64)
3. Read the circuit as local thermal noise.
By the commutation of the two kinds of beam splitters proved in
Lemma 3, the second circuit order has the same
four-output state  $\Xi$ . Immediately after the  $\eta$ -beam splitters,
the state is
$\omega_{CE}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{C}}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{E}}.$
(65)
Mix  $E,G_{E}$  on the balanced beam splitter and retain  $J:=E_{+}$ .
The state before mixing  $C,G_{C}$  is
$\sigma_{CJ}\otimes(\tau_{2})_{G_{C}},\qquad\sigma_{CJ}=(\operatorname{id}_{C}\otimes\Phi)(\omega_{CE}).$
(66)
The auxiliary  $G_{C}$  is independent of the entire pair  $CJ$  because it
is a separate factor in (65). After the remaining
balanced beam splitter, the  $C_{+}J$  marginal is
$\Xi_{C_{+}J}=(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{J})(\sigma_{CJ}).$
(67)
4. Convert zero conditional information into zero channel loss.
Independence of  $G_{C}$  and unitary invariance give
$\displaystyle I(C_{+}C_{-};J)_{\Xi}$
$\displaystyle=I(CG_{C};J)_{\sigma\otimes\tau_{2}}$
$\displaystyle=S(\sigma_{C})+S(\tau_{2})+S(\sigma_{J})-S(\sigma_{CJ})-S(\tau_{2})$
$\displaystyle=I(C;J)_{\sigma}.$
(68)
On the other hand, the chain rule and (64) give
$\displaystyle I(C_{+}C_{-};J)_{\Xi}$
$\displaystyle=I(C_{+};J)_{\Xi}+I(C_{-};J\mid C_{+})_{\Xi}=I(C_{+};J)_{\Xi}.$
(69)
Combining these identities with (67) yields
$I(C;J)_{\sigma}=I(C_{+};J)_{(\Phi\otimes\operatorname{id}_{J})(\sigma)}.$
(70)
Proposition 6 applies because  $\sigma_{C}=\omega_{C}$
has finite energy and  $S(\sigma_{J})<\infty$ . It makes  $\sigma_{CJ}$  a product. Its marginals are
$\sigma_{C}=\omega_{C}$  and  $\sigma_{J}=\Phi(\omega_{E})$ , so
$(\operatorname{id}_{C}\otimes\Phi)(\omega_{CE})=\omega_{C}\otimes\Phi(\omega_{E}).$
(71)
5. Remove the noise on the other output.
For  $u,w\in\mathbb{C}^{m}$ , write
$\widehat{\omega}(u,w)=\operatorname{Tr}\omega_{CE}[\mathcal{D}_{C}(u)\otimes\mathcal{D}_{E}(w)]$ .
The channel formula (44) applies also to one
factor of a joint state. Equation (71) therefore gives
$\widehat{\omega}(u,w/\sqrt{2})e^{-5|w|^{2}/4}=\widehat{\omega}_{C}(u)\widehat{\omega}_{E}(w/\sqrt{2})e^{-5|w|^{2}/4}.$
The multiplier is nonzero, and  $w\mapsto w/\sqrt{2}$  is onto  $\mathbb{C}^{m}$ .
Cancelling it yields
$\widehat{\omega}(u,v)=\widehat{\omega}_{C}(u)\widehat{\omega}_{E}(v)\quad(u,v\in\mathbb{C}^{m}).$
Uniqueness of Weyl characteristic functions now proves
$\omega_{CE}=\omega_{C}\otimes\omega_{E}$ .
∎
3.5 Gaussian characterization and the converse
Equation (5) already gives (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (i),
because its two deficits are nonnegative.
Proof of (ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii).
The finite-energy quantum Darmois–Skitovich characterization,
Proposition 14, applies to the independent inputs and
product outputs. It gives Gaussianity and equality of covariance
matrices. Appendix B gives the full proof by reducing each
quadrature direction to two independent scalar random variables.
Their orthogonal mixtures are independent, which forces Gaussian laws
with equal variances. The means remain unrestricted.
∎
Proof of (iii) $\Rightarrow$ (i), including product outputs.
Let the Gaussian inputs have covariance  $V$  and means  $d_{A},d_{B}$ .
Set  $a=\sqrt{\eta}$ ,  $b=\sqrt{1-\eta}$ . The Gaussian output has

5 Discussion
The equality condition for the bosonic qEPI can be expressed entirely
in terms of the two output systems: an independent finite-energy pair
attains either entropy inequality precisely when its beam-splitter
outputs are independent. The Gaussian characterization then follows
from the quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem. The thermal auxiliary is
what connects an entropy condition on one output to this structural
condition on both outputs.
The method also separates two roles of Gaussian states. The auxiliary
thermal states are introduced at a fixed finite energy to obtain strict
information loss. The Gaussian limit in the exponential proof serves
a different purpose: it determines the affine weight and the input
covariances. The linear equality proof is complete before that limit
argument is used.

Proposition 14 (Finite-energy quantum characterization).
If independent finite-energy  $m$ -mode inputs have independent outputs under
a beam splitter with  $0<\eta<1$ , they are Gaussian with equal covariance
matrices and arbitrary displacement vectors.
Proof.
Fix any real vector  $\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{2m}$ . The self-adjoint quadrature
$\xi^{T}R_{A}$  has a classical spectral law in state  $\rho_{A}$ : its probability
of a Borel set  $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}$  is
$\operatorname{Tr}\rho_{A}\mathbf{1}_{B}(\xi^{T}R_{A})$ , where  $\mathbf{1}_{B}(\xi^{T}R_{A})$  is its
spectral projection. Let  $X$  have this law, and let  $Y$  have the corresponding
law for  $\xi^{T}R_{B}$ . Their joint law in the product input is the independent
product of these two laws. Both second moments are finite; this follows
from the quadratic-form interpretation of (7) and
$\operatorname{Tr}\rho R_{j}^{2}<\infty$ .
The two operators  $\xi^{T}R_{A}$  and  $\xi^{T}R_{B}$  act on different tensor factors,
so their spectral measures commute. Their two linear combinations therefore
have the ordinary joint law of
$aX+bY$  and  $-bX+aY$ , where  $a=\sqrt{\eta}$ ,  $b=\sqrt{1-\eta}$ .
By (1), this is also the joint spectral law of
$\xi^{T}R_{C}$  and  $\xi^{T}R_{E}$  in the output state. Product outputs make these
laws independent. Lemma 13 applies.
Thus, for each  $\xi$ ,  $X$  is Gaussian with mean  $\xi^{T}d_{A}$  and variance
$\xi^{T}V_{A}\xi$ , and  $Y$  is Gaussian with mean  $\xi^{T}d_{B}$  and the same
variance. Evaluating their scalar characteristic functions at one gives
$\chi_{A}(\xi)=e^{i\xi^{T}d_{A}-\xi^{T}V_{A}\xi/2},\qquad\chi_{B}(\xi)=e^{i\xi^{T}d_{B}-\xi^{T}V_{B}\xi/2}.$
(102)
These hold for every  $\xi$ , so the definition (12)
proves Gaussianity. The equality
$\xi^{T}(V_{A}-V_{B})\xi=0$  for every real  $\xi$  implies  $V_{A}=V_{B}$  by
polarization of real quadratic forms. This is the finite-energy instance
of the exact quantum Darmois–Skitovich theorem [8, Theorem 7].

II.2 Stability
In the last section we presented an exact version of the DS theorem which brings naturally an operational characterization of Gaussian bosonic states. There, it is assumed an exact factorizability of the output state. In practice, it is impossible to assure such thesis since there are always errors in the measurements and therefore the validity of the result is not completely clear in real life. Moreover, any practical application can be inmmediatealy rule out if the conclusion is not robust against small changes in the defined conditions.
We are interested in finding to which extent the results of theorem 7 are affected if the main assumption is not exact but approximately satisfied. Before specifying the conditions of the stability of the quantum DS theorem, we briefly comment on the respective classical stability problem[11].
The stability of the classical DS theorem is due to Yu. R. Gabovich [15]. In his work, the word “approximately” is quantified in terms of the closeness of the cumulative distribution functions of the random variables. It is shown (Theorem 3 in Ref. 15) that for approximate independency the considered classical probability distributions are  $c(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))^{-1/8}$ -close to a normal distribution in the Levy metric. In this estimate there is no explicit value of the constant  $c$  and therefore it is not known how it depends on the coefficients of the linear forms, neither on the number of random variables involved.
At the level of density operators it was proven[16] that weak operator topology is equivalent to trace-norm topology.
Therefore Gabovich result and corollary 2 should imply at least in a qualitative manner that the quantum DS theorem is stable. However, we can obtain a better concrete estimate of the stability of the DS theorem by considering not just the marginals and the classical result, but rather using the entire phase space and the natural restrictions on the quantum characteristic functions. Namely, due to Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle there cannot be characteristic functions which are highly concentrated in some region of phase space. This naturally rules out ill-behaved distributions that can appear in the classical case. With no more preambules, we give a precise statement of our result.
We say that a quantum state  $\rho_{ab}$  is an  $\varepsilon-$ approximate product state if there is a product state  $\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b}$  such that
$\left\lVert\rho_{ab}-\rho_{a}\otimes\rho_{b}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon,$

III.3 Proof of the stability of DS theorem 9
The proof involves a series of steps. We first use Parseval’s theorem to express the distance of the quantum states in terms of the  $L_{2}-$ distance of their respective characteristic functions. Next, we show that there is a ball  $\mathfrak{B}_{r}$  around the origin of phase space where the characteristic functions do not vanish. The radius of this ball scales inversely proportional to the largest variance of the input states and proportional to  $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ . Thus the smaller the error parameter  $\varepsilon$  the bigger this region is. We then proceed to bound the distance separately on  $\mathfrak{B}_{r}$  and its complement  $\mathfrak{B}^{c}_{r}$ . For the latter region, we exploit the relation between the tails of a distribution and the finiteness of it moments. Inside  $\mathfrak{B}_{r}$ , the problem is equivalent to the stability of the Gaussian functional Eq. (19) with restricted convex domain. For that matter, the stability of the Gaussian functional equation is reduced to the stability of the fundamental functional equation, namely the Cauchy functional equation.
We may assumed without lost of generality that the input states (and therefore the output states) are centered. This is justified by the fact that the trace and HS norms are unitarily invariant and the operation of “Gaussification” (the operation on bosonic quantum states which produces Gaussian states with the same first and second moments of the input state) commutes with the displacement operation  $\rho\mapsto W_{d}\rho W^{*}_{d}$ .
We denote by  $\chi_{ab},\chi_{a}$  and  $\chi_{b}$  the characteristic functions of  $\rho_{ab},\rho_{a}$  and  $\rho_{b}$ , respectively. From Lemma (17), we have

Bound inside the region where  $\chi$  does not vanish:
We proceed to compute the bound for the first term of the RHS of Eq. (40) following the ideas of Ref. 13, 14, 15. For that matter, let
$\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\in\reals^{2n}$  with  $\left\lVert\eta_{j}\right\rVert_{2}<r/2$  so that  $\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2},\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1}\in\mathfrak{B}_{r}$ .
Let us take the logarithm (principal branch) on both sides of Eq. (37). We write
$\Psi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\Psi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\Psi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})+\Psi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\Psi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})+\Psi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})+Q(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}),$
(50)
where  $\Psi_{j}(\eta):=-\log\chi_{j}(\eta)$  for  $j=1,2$  and
$Q(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=-\log\left(1+\frac{G(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})}{\chi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})\chi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})}\right).$
(51)
Since  $\rho_{j},j=1,2$  is Schwartz, we can define continuous vector-valued functions  $\phi_{j}(\xi):\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n}$  by
$\phi_{j}(\xi):=\nabla\Psi_{j}(\xi).$
Note that  $\phi_{j}(\xi),j=1,2,$  are in fact conservative vector fields and that  $\phi_{j}(0)=0$  as  $\rho_{j}$  is centered. The gradient of  $\phi_{j}$  is the Hessian of  $\chi_{j}$  (see Lemma 14) and  $2\nabla\phi_{j}(0)=\sigma\varGamma_{j}\sigma^{T}$  for  $j=1,2$ .
Inhomogeneous Cauchy Functional Equation
Next, we want to obtain a functional equation only depending on  $\chi_{1}$  or  $\chi_{2}$ . In order to
do so, we differentiate Eq. (50) in the direction of  $\eta_{1}$  to find
$\cos\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\sin\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\cos\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\sin\theta\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})+Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}),$
(52)
where  $Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=\frac{dQ(\eta_{1}+t\eta_{1},\eta_{2})}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}$ . We evaluate in Eq. (52)  $\eta_{1}=0$  to get
$\cos\theta\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\sin\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})=Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2}),$
(53)
In a similar fashion we differentiate Eq. (50) in the direction of  $\eta_{2}$  and set to zero to obtain
$\sin\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\cos\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=\sin\theta\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})+\cos\theta\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})+Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}),$
(54)
$\sin\theta\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})+\cos\theta\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})=Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0),$
(55)
where
$Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}):=\frac{dQ(\eta_{1},\eta_{2}+t\eta_{2})}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}$ .
Now we will be able to decouple  $\phi_{1}$  and  $\phi_{2}$ . First, we substract Eq. (53) from Eq. (52) and Eq. (55) from Eq. (54) to obtain
$\begin{split}[\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})]&=\tan\theta[\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})]\\
&+\frac{Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2})}{\cos\theta},\end{split}$
(56)
$\begin{split}[\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})]&=-\tan\theta[\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})]\\
&+\frac{Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0)}{\cos\theta}.\end{split}$
(57)
Thus from Eq. (56) and (57) we find the following inhomogeneous Cauchy equations
$\begin{split}[\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1}+\sin\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{1}(\sin\theta\eta_{2})]&=\sin\theta[Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0)]\\
&+\cos\theta[Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2})],\end{split}$
(58)
$\begin{split}[\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2}-\sin\theta\eta_{1})-\phi_{2}(\cos\theta\eta_{2})-\phi_{2}(-\sin\theta\eta_{1})]&=\sin\theta[Q_{1}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{1}(0,\eta_{2})]\\
&+\cos\theta[Q_{2}(\eta_{1},\eta_{2})-Q_{2}(\eta_{1},0)].\end{split}$
(59)
Bound on  $\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}$
Now that  $\phi_{1}$  and  $\phi_{2}$  are decoupled, we continue only with  $\phi_{1}$  as with  $\phi_{2}$  is analogous and the same upper bound is obtained. We recall that the derivative of a vector with respect to a vector can be represented as a matrix. Thus when we differentiate Eq. (58) in the direction of  $\eta_{2}$  and evaluate at  $\eta_{2}=0$ , we obtain the following matrix-valued equation
$\nabla\phi_{1}(\cos\theta\eta_{1})-\frac{\sigma\varGamma_{1}\sigma^{T}}{2}+\frac{Q_{12}(0,0)}{\tan\theta}=Q_{22}(\eta_{1})+\frac{Q_{12}(\eta_{1})}{\tan\theta}.$
(60)
Here  $Q_{12}(\eta_{1},0):\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n}$  and  $Q_{22}(\eta_{1},0):\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n}$  are defined as
$Q_{12}(\eta_{1},0):=\frac{\partial^{2}Q(\eta_{1}+t\eta_{1},s\eta_{2})}{\partial s\partial t}\Bigr|_{s=t=0}\qquad\text{and}\qquad Q_{22}(\eta_{1}):=\frac{\partial^{2}Q(\eta_{1},s\eta_{2}+t\eta_{2})}{\partial s\partial t}\Bigr|_{s=t=0}.$
(61)
Accordingly, we integrate the previous equation twice from zero to  $\eta$ ,  $\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{2}\leq r/2$ . We obtain for  $\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}$
$\chi_{1}(\xi)=\exp[-\xi\cdot\left(\frac{\sigma\varGamma_{1}\sigma^{T}}{4}-\frac{V}{2}\right)\xi-F\left(\frac{\xi}{\cos\theta}\right)],$
(62)
with
$V:=-\frac{Q_{12}(0,0)}{\tan\theta}=\frac{\sigma(\Tr gR_{1}R_{2}^{T})\sigma^{T}}{\tan\theta},$
$F(\xi):=\cos^{2}\theta\int_{\mathcal{C}(\xi)}\left(\int_{\mathcal{C}(\eta)}\left(Q_{22}(\eta_{1})+\frac{Q_{12}(\eta_{1})}{\tan\theta}\right)\cdot d\eta_{1}\right)\cdot d\eta,$
where  $\mathcal{C}(\xi),\mathcal{C}(\eta)$  are curves in phase space connecting the origin with the vectors  $\xi$  and  $\eta$ . Moreover, these last terms can be upper bounded by (see Appendix on section V)
$\displaystyle\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{\sqrt{24n^{2}\kappa}}{|\tan\theta|}\right)\sqrt{\varepsilon},$
(63)
$\displaystyle\left|F\left(\frac{\xi}{\cos\theta}\right)\right|^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{n^{2}\kappa\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}}{2\tan^{2}\theta}\right)\varepsilon^{2/3},$
(64)
where the largest absolute fourth moment of  $\rho_{ab}$  is defined as
$\kappa:=\max\left\{\left\lVert\rho_{ab}R^{2}_{\xi}R^{2}_{\eta}\right\rVert_{1}\;\big|\;\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}=\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert_{2}=1\right\}.$
(65)
At this point we can show that the CM of  $\rho_{1}$  and  $\rho_{2}$  are  $\varepsilon-$ close. From differentiating Eq. (53) with respect to  $\eta_{2}$  and evaluating at zero,
we get the relation between the CMs of  $\rho_{1}$  and  $\rho_{2}$ ,
$\varGamma_{1}-\varGamma_{2}=\frac{2}{\cos^{2}\theta}V.$
Hence, from Eq. (63)
$\left\lVert\varGamma_{1}-\varGamma_{2}\right\rVert_{2}\leq\left(\frac{\sqrt{384n^{2}\kappa}}{|\sin 2\theta|}\right)\ \sqrt{\varepsilon}.$
(66)
Now we can proceed to show that for  $\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}$ , the characteristic function of the state  $\rho_{1}$  is  $\varepsilon-$ close to the Gaussian characteristic
function  $\Phi=\exp[-\xi\cdot\varGamma_{1}\xi/4]$ .
We use Eq. (62),  $|e^{x}-1|\leq|x|\max\left\{1,e^{\operatorname{Re}[x]}\right\}$  and  $|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}=|\Phi(\xi)|^{2}e^{\xi\cdot V\xi-2\operatorname{Re}[F(\xi/\cos\theta)]}$  to write the bound as
$\displaystyle\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi$
$\displaystyle=\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\Phi(\xi)|^{2}|\exp[\xi\cdot V\xi/2-F(\xi/\cos\theta)]-1\right|^{2}d\xi$
$\displaystyle\leq\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left|\frac{\xi\cdot V\xi}{2}-F(\xi/\cos\theta)\right|^{2}d\xi,$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left(\frac{|\xi\cdot V\xi|^{2}}{4}+|F(\xi/\cos\theta)|^{2}\right)d\xi$
$\displaystyle\leq\left(\frac{4n^{2}\kappa\varepsilon^{2/3}}{\tan^{2}\theta}\right)\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi,$
(67)
Here in the second inequality we have used again  $|z_{1}-z_{2}|^{2}\leq(|z_{1}|^{2}+|z_{2}|^{2})/2$  for  $z_{1},z_{2}\in\mathbb{C}$  and in the last inequality Eq. (63) and Eq. (64). We show now that
$\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi\leq\frac{512n^{2}\kappa}{\pi^{n}}\left(\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\cos^{4}\theta}\right).$
(68)
We used again the Wigner representation, Eq.(43), of the characteristic function  $|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}$  in order to compute the bound of Eq. (68)
$\displaystyle\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}^{4}d\xi,$
$\displaystyle=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\ \int\limits_{\xi\in\reals^{2n}}|\chi_{1}(\xi)|^{2}\xi^{2}_{k}\xi^{2}_{l}d\xi,$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\partial^{4}\mathcal{W}(0)}{\partial\eta^{2}_{k}\partial\eta^{2}_{l}}.$
Using Lemma 14 with the help of the CCR gives
$\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\frac{\partial^{4}\mathcal{W}(0)}{\partial\eta^{2}_{k}\partial\eta^{2}_{l}}=\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\Tr[\rho\mathcal{P}\{R^{2}_{k},R^{2}_{l}\}].$
Here  $\rho$  is again the density operator corresponding to the characteristic function  $|\chi(\xi)|^{2}$ . We use again that  $\mathcal{P}\rho=\rho\mathcal{P}$  (see subsection III.3) and Hölder’s inequality to bound
$\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\Tr[\rho\mathcal{P}\{R^{2}_{k},R^{2}_{l}\}]\leq\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\left(\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}R^{2}_{k}R^{2}_{l}\sqrt{\rho}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\sqrt{\rho}R^{2}_{l}R^{2}_{k}\sqrt{\rho}\right\rVert_{1}\right).$
Now using Cauchy-Schwartz inequality and the ciclycity properties for Schwartz operators we find
$\displaystyle\frac{8}{\pi^{n}}\sum_{k,l=1}^{2n}\Tr[\rho\mathcal{P}\{R^{2}_{k},R^{2}_{l}\}]$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{16}{\pi^{n}}\left(\sum^{2n}_{k=1}(\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k})^{1/2}\right)^{2},$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{32n}{\pi^{n}}\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k}.$
(69)
Since we want to specify all the constants in terms of the moments of the output state  $\rho_{ab}$  we need to do the following computations. Using the explicit form of the BS transformation Eq. (18) and the derivatives of  $\chi_{1}(\xi)$ , we obtain after a tedious, but straightforward calculation
$\cos^{4}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{1k}+\sin^{4}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{2}R^{4}_{2k}-6\sin^{2}\theta\cos^{2}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{1k}\Tr\rho_{2}R^{2}_{2k}=\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{k},$
which together with the positivity of the fourth moments implies
$\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{k}\leq 6\tan^{2}\theta\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{1k}\Tr\rho_{2}R^{2}_{2k}+\frac{1}{\cos^{4}\theta}\sum^{2n}_{k=1}\Tr\rho_{ab}R^{4}_{k}.$
(70)
Moreover, the relation between the fourth moments of the symmetrized state  $\rho$  and  $\rho_{1}$  is given by
$\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k}=2\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{k}+6(\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{k})^{2},\qquad k=1,\ldots,2n.$
(71)
Combining Eqs. (70) and (71) and using  $(\Tr\rho_{1}R^{2}_{k})^{2}\leq\Tr\rho_{1}R^{4}_{k}\leq\kappa$  we obtain
$\sum_{k=1}^{2n}\Tr\rho R^{4}_{k}\leq 16n\kappa\left(\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\cos^{4}\theta}\right),$
and Eq. (69) gives the claimed bound in Eq. (68). Hence, inserting Eq. (68) in Eq. (67) we obtain the bound for the non-vanishing region  $\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}$
$\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n}}\int\limits_{\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}}\left|\chi_{1}(\xi)-\Phi(\xi)\right|^{2}d\xi\leq c^{2}_{1}\varepsilon^{2/3},$
(72)
where
$c_{1}:=32\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi^{n}}\left(\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\sin 2\theta}\right)}n^{2}\kappa.$
(73)
Figure 3: Dependence of the stability constant  $c_{1}$  in terms of the transmission coefficient  $\theta$ . The  $y-$ axis is the function  $\sqrt{\frac{1+3\sin 2\theta}{\sin 2\theta}}$ . The constant  $c_{1}(\theta,n,\kappa)$  for the one mode 50-50 BS case is  $c_{1}\approx 46.2\kappa.$
The result of the theorem follows from Eq. (48), (72) and the concavity of the square root.
IV Discussion
The DS theorem can be understood as the statement that Gaussian bosonic states with same covariance matrix are the only fixed point states of a non-trivial beam splitter transformation. In constrast with other characterizations of Gaussian states such as the one from Hudson[12], the DS theorem does not require any constraint on the purity of the state. The stability result of Theorem 9 provides an explicit estimate of the robustness of a characterization of Gaussian states through linear independence. In particular, we have obtained an estimate of the constants which reflect the fact that the quantum DS theorem is unstable when the beam-splitter is close to being transparent ( $\theta=0$ ) or a mirror ( $\theta=\pi/2$ ). The exact dependence on the transmitivity constant is shown in Fig. 3. Throughout this work, we have made an effort to present explicit constants as well as to improve the order of the error parameter; however this does not mean that they are anywhere close to optimal. In fact, it is not known to us if the optimal constant must necessarily depend on the number of modes  $n$  or whether the  $\log(1/\varepsilon)^{-1/2}$  dependence can be lifted to a polynomial dependence.
The Darmois-Skitovich theorem is not only interesting as a neat characterization problem, but also because of its practical applications: it is the main theoretical concept behind the signal reconstruction method known as blind source separation[18] which is actively studied in the field of communication and signal processing. We hope with this study of the stability of the quantum DS theorem to stimulate a further investigation of this theorem and its extensions in the quantum information community.
IV.1 Auxiliary Lemmas
Lemma 16.
Let  $S\in GL(4n,\mathbb{R})$  such that
$S\begin{pmatrix}{}\varGamma&0\\
0&\varGamma\end{pmatrix}S^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cdot&0\\
0&*\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{is $2n\times 2n$ block diagonal for all symmetric $\varGamma\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$.}$
(74)
Then it follows that:
(i)
$S$  is either of the form
(a)
$S=\begin{pmatrix}{}A&0\\
0&D\end{pmatrix}$  or  $S=\begin{pmatrix}{}0&B\\
C&0\end{pmatrix}$ ,
(b)
$S=\begin{pmatrix}{}A&B\\
C&D\end{pmatrix}$ ,
with  $A,B,C$  and  $D\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$  invertible.
(ii)
$S\begin{pmatrix}{}X&0\\
0&X\end{pmatrix}S^{T}=\begin{pmatrix}{}\cdot&0\\
0&*\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{is $2n\times 2n$ block diagonal for all $X\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$.}$
(75)
Proof of Lemma 16.
We decompose  $S=\begin{pmatrix}{}A&B\\
C&D\end{pmatrix}$  into blocks  $A,B,C$  and  $D\in\reals^{n\times n}$  and observe that
equation (74) is equivalent to
$A\varGamma C^{T}+B\varGamma D^{T}=0\quad\text{for all $\varGamma=\varGamma^{T}$.}$
(76)
Using tensor notation this equation can be written[20] as
$\displaystyle(A\otimes C+B\otimes D)|\varGamma\rangle=0\quad\quad\text{for all $|\varGamma\rangle\in\mathbb{R}^{4n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{4n}$ symmetric}.$
$\displaystyle\iff$
$\displaystyle(A\otimes C+B\otimes D)P_{+}|X\rangle=0\quad\quad\text{for all $|X\rangle\in\mathbb{R}^{4n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{4n}$.}$
$\displaystyle\iff$
$\displaystyle(A\otimes C+B\otimes D)P_{+}=0.$
$\iff P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes C^{T}+B^{T}\otimes D^{T})=0,$
(77)
where  $P_{+}$  denotes the projector onto the symmetric subspace of  $\mathbb{R}^{4n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{4n}$ .
We make the following remark that will be used frequently during this proof:
the symmetrization or symmetric component of a non-zero product state does not vanish. Suppose it does, then  $P_{+}(|v\rangle\otimes|w\rangle)=0$  and
$|v\rangle\otimes|w\rangle+|w\rangle\otimes|v\rangle=0$ . Performing the scalar product with  $\langle v|\otimes\langle w|$
leads to  $\left\lVert v\right\rVert^{2}\left\lVert w\right\rVert^{2}+|\langle v|w\rangle|^{2}=0$  which is only zero if and only if  $|v\rangle=|w\rangle=0$ .
On (i): We now prove the first part of the Lemma by considering the two cases:
(a) One of the submatrices  $A$ , $B$ , $C$  or  $D$  is zero: we only treat the case  $A=0$ , the others are similar.
Then  $A^{T}\otimes C^{T}=0$  and  $B^{T}$  is invertible (otherwise  $S$  would not have full rank). Since any non-zero product
$B^{T}v\otimes D^{T}w$  (for some  $v,w\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ ) would contain a non-vanishing symmetric component,
equation (77) implies that  $D^{T}=0$ .
(b) We prove by contradiction that in this case the four submatrices are invertible. For instance, assume that  $A$  is not invertible. Then there exists
a vector  $0\neq|a\rangle\in\text{Ker}A^{T}$ . We choose  $|e\rangle\notin\text{Ker}D^{T}$  (recall that  $D\neq 0$ ) and with (77) we then find
$0=P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes C^{T}+B^{T}\otimes D^{T})|a\rangle\otimes|e\rangle=P_{+}(B^{T}|a\rangle\otimes D^{T}|e\rangle).$
(78)
By the same argument as in  $(a)$  we now conclude  $|a\rangle\in\text{Ker}B^{T}$ . Moreover,
$S^{T}\begin{pmatrix}a\\
0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A^{T}&C^{T}\\
B^{T}&D^{T}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\
0\end{pmatrix}=0.$
The latter is in contradiction to the invertibility of  $S$  (if  $S$  is an invertible matrix then the kernel is trivial),
hence A –and due to analogous reasoning–  $B,C$  and  $D$  are invertible.
On (ii): We now proof the second part of the Lemma, Eq. (75), by showing
that the equivalent expression  $AXC^{T}+BXD^{T}=0$
for all  $X\in\mathbb{R}^{2n\times 2n}$  is true.
This is trivially satisfied if  $S$  is given in form of case (i,a). Therefore we are left with the case (i,b) where in particular  $B$  and  $C$  are invertible.
W.l.o.g. we choose  $B=C=\iden$  (this can be done by redefining  $A\to A^{-1}B$  and  $D\to D^{-1}C$  in (76))
and equation (77) reads
$P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T})=0.$
(79)
We now show in three steps that  $A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T}=0$ , which then concludes the proof.
First we show that there exists  $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$  such that  $Spec(A^{T})=\{\lambda\}$  and  $Spec(D^{T})=\{-\lambda\}$ .
To this purpose we choose
eigenvectors  $|e\rangle$  of  $A^{T}$  and  $|f\rangle$  of and  $D^{T}$  with eigenvalues  $\lambda$  and  $\omega$  respectively. Then
$0=P_{+}(A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T})|e\rangle\otimes|f\rangle=(\lambda+\omega)P_{+}(|e\rangle\otimes|f\rangle).$
Again, since the symmetrization of a non-zero product state is different from zero, we find  $\lambda=-\omega$ . Note that this holds for arbitrary
eigenvalues  $\lambda$  of  $A^{T}$  and  $\omega$  of  $D^{T}$ .
Second, using the Jordan normal form decomposition, we decompose  $A^{T}$  (and  $D^{T}$ ) into a diagonalizable  $\lambda\iden$  and nilpotent part  $N_{A}(N_{D})$
and observe that  $(A^{T}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes D^{T})=(\lambda\iden\otimes\iden+N_{A}\otimes\iden)+\iden\otimes(-\lambda\iden+N_{D})=(N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D})$ .
Finally, equation (79) reads
$P_{+}(N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D})=0,$
(80)
and we can conclude the proof by deriving that this implies  $(N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D})=0$ . This is the third step.
Assume  $N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D}\neq 0$ . Using the symmetry argument about non-zero product states we find
$N_{A}\neq 0$  and  $N_{D}\neq 0$ .
Let  $s$  be such that  $N_{A}^{s}=0$  and  $N_{A}^{s-1}\neq 0$ . Then we multiply (80) from the right by  $N_{A}^{s-1}\otimes\iden$  to get  $P_{+}(N_{A}^{s-1}\otimes N_{D})=0$ .
But this, in turn, implies  $N_{A}^{s}\otimes N_{D}=0$  and leads to a contradiction. Therefore
$(N_{A}\otimes\iden+\iden\otimes N_{D})=0.$
(81)
∎
Lemma 17.
Let  $\rho_{12}$  be a density operator of a bipartite system with reduced states  $\rho_{1}$  and  $\rho_{2}$ . If  $\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}$  describe an arbitrary product state and  $\left\lVert\rho_{12}-\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\varepsilon$ , then
$\left\lVert\rho_{12}-\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}\leq 3\varepsilon$ .
Proof.
Using the triangle inequality twice, we find
$\displaystyle\left\lVert\rho_{12}-\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}$
$\displaystyle\leq\left\lVert\rho_{12}-\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1},$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\rho_{2}-\rho_{1}\otimes\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1},$
$\displaystyle=\varepsilon+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{2}\right\rVert_{1}+\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}-\rho_{1}\right\rVert_{1}.$
Exploiting that  $\left\lVert X\right\rVert_{1}=\sup_{Y:\left\lVert Y\right\rVert\leq 1}\ \Tr[YX]$  we can bound
$\displaystyle\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}-\rho_{1}\right\rVert_{1}$
$\displaystyle=\sup_{Y:\left\lVert Y\right\rVert\leq 1}\ \Tr[(Y\otimes\iden)(\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{12})],$
$\displaystyle\leq\sup_{\hat{Y}:\left\lVert\hat{Y}\right\rVert\leq 1}\ \Tr[\hat{Y}(\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{12})],$
$\displaystyle=\left\lVert\tilde{\rho_{1}}\otimes\tilde{\rho_{2}}-\rho_{12}\right\rVert_{1}\leq\epsilon,$
and similar for the other term.

Proof of Lemma (15).
We follow the proof idea of Lemma 1 from Ref. 15.
W.l.o.g assume  $0<\theta\leq\pi/4$  and set  $\eta_{2}=\tan\theta\eta_{1},\eta_{1}=\xi$  in Eq. 37. In case  $\theta>\pi/4$ , set  $\eta_{1}=\eta_{2}/\tan\theta$  in Eq. 37 and proceed likewise. Then Eq. 37 becomes
$\chi_{1}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\cos\theta\xi\right)=\chi_{1}\left(\cos\theta\xi\right)\chi_{1}(\sin\theta\tan\theta\xi)\chi_{2}(\cos\theta\tan\theta\xi)\chi_{2}(-\sin\theta\xi)+G(\xi,\tan\theta\xi),$
for all  $\xi\in\reals^{2n}$ . Replace  $\xi\mapsto(\xi/\cos\theta)$  in the previous equation to obtain
$\chi_{1}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)=\chi_{1}\left(\xi\right)\chi_{1}(\tan^{2}\theta\xi)|\chi_{2}(\tan\theta\xi)|^{2}+G\left(\frac{\xi}{\cos\theta},\frac{\tan\theta\xi}{\cos\theta}\right).$
Since  $\left\lVert G\right\rVert\leq 3\varepsilon$ , we have for all  $\xi\in\reals^{2n}$ :
$\left|\chi_{1}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)\right|\geq|\chi_{1}(\xi)||\chi_{1}(\tan^{2}\theta\xi)||\chi_{2}(\tan\theta\xi)|^{2}-3\varepsilon.$
Similarly, for  $0<\theta\leq\pi/4$  and  $\eta_{1}=-\tan\theta\eta_{2},\eta_{2}=\xi$  we arrive to
$\left|\chi_{2}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)\right|\geq|\chi_{2}(\xi)||\chi_{2}(\tan^{2}\theta\xi)||\chi_{1}(\tan\theta\xi)|^{2}-3\varepsilon.$
With  $\gamma(\xi):=\min_{j}\min_{\left\lVert\eta\right\rVert<\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert}\left|\chi_{j}(\eta)\right|$  we obtain
$\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)\xi\right)\geq\gamma^{4}\left(\xi\right)-3\varepsilon$ .
Replacing  $\xi$  by  $\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k}\xi$  with  $k\in\mathbb{N}$  in the previous equation gives
$\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k+1}\xi\right)\geq\gamma^{4}\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k}\xi\right)-3\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }\xi\in\reals^{2n},k\in\mathbb{N}.$
(82)
It is a fact that for any classical characteristic function  $\phi(t)$  with variance  $\lambda$  the following inequality holds (see for instance Ref. 17, p. 89)
$|\phi(t)|\geq 1-\frac{1}{2}\lambda t^{2}.$
(83)
Let us fix  $\xi$  in the direction of phase space in which we obtain the largest variance  $\lambda$  of  $\rho_{1}$  and  $\rho_{2}$
and consider the region where  $\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}$ . Then from Eq. 83 for  $\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}$  we have  $|\chi(\xi)|\geq 1/2$ .
Using Eq. (82) and the inequality  $(1-a)^{n}\geq 1-na,\forall n\in\mathbb{N},\forall a\in[0,1]$ , we can show by induction that
$\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k+1}\xi\right)\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4^{k}}-4\varepsilon\qquad\text{for }k\in\mathbb{N},\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}.$
Moreover, for  $\varepsilon<1$  we clearly have
$\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k+1}\xi\right)\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4^{k}}-4\varepsilon^{1/12}\qquad\text{for }k\in\mathbb{N},\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert_{2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{\lambda}}.$
(84)
Finally, we take  $k_{0}$  such that  $2^{k_{0}}=\sqrt{\log_{2}\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{1/12}}}$ , to obtain with the help of Eq. (84)
$\displaystyle\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k_{0}}\xi\right)$
$\displaystyle\geq\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4^{k_{0}-1}}-4\varepsilon^{1/12},$
$\displaystyle=12\varepsilon^{1/12}.$
We thus have  $\gamma\left(\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k_{0}}\xi\right)>\varepsilon^{1/12}$  and  $\left(1+\tan^{2}\theta\right)^{k_{0}}\xi\in\mathfrak{B}_{r}$  as claimed.

V.1 Upper bound of  $\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2}$ , Eq. 63.
Let us write  $R_{1k},k=1,\ldots 2n,$  and  $R_{2l},l=1,\ldots 2n,$  for the entries of the vector  $R_{1}=(Q_{1},P_{1},\ldots,Q_{n},P_{n})$  and  $R_{2}=(Q_{n+1},P_{n+1},\ldots,Q_{2n},P_{2n})$  respectively. First, from the orthogonality of the symplectic matrix  $\sigma$
$\displaystyle\left\lVert V\right\rVert_{2}$
$\displaystyle=\frac{\left\lVert\sigma(\Tr gR_{1}R_{2}^{T})\sigma^{T}\right\rVert_{2}}{|\tan\theta|}$

Our plan is to bound each entry  $|\Tr gR_{1k}R_{2l}|^{2}$ . Since the operator  $g$  is the difference of two Schwartz operators it is also Schwartz. If  $g=\sum\lambda_{i}|i\rangle\langle i|$  is the spectral decomposition of  $g$ , we consider the following factorization
$g=|g|Q,\qquad\text{with}\qquad Q:=\sum_{i}\sgn(\lambda_{i})|i\rangle\langle i|.$
Clearly,  $Q=Q^{-1}$  commutes with  $|g|$  and  $|g|^{1/2}$ .

$\displaystyle\leq(3\varepsilon)\max\{\Tr|g|R^{4}_{1k},\Tr|g|R^{4}_{2l}\}.$

$\int A\cdot d\eta:=\begin{pmatrix}\int A_{1}\cdot d\eta\\
\vdots\\
\int A_{2n}\cdot d\eta\end{pmatrix}.$
Thus the line integral of a matrix-valued function is a vector, and the line integral of a vector field is a scalar.
Let us denote by  $M:\reals^{2n}\to\mathbb{C}^{2n\times 2n}$  a matrix-valued function. The upper bound for Eq. 64 is equivalent to bound
$F(\xi):=\int_{\mathcal{C}(\xi)}\left(\int_{\mathcal{C}(\eta)}M(z)\cdot dz\right)\cdot d\eta,$
with  $\xi,\eta\in\mathfrak{B}_{r/2}$  and

For a channel  $\mathcal{N}$ , let
$P_{\mathrm{s}}^{\star}(n,r;\mathcal{N})$  denote the optimal average
decoding success probability over  $n$  uses with at least  $2^{nr}$  messages.
We allow arbitrary entangled input codewords and collective
decoding, but no entanglement assistance.
The strong-converse exponent is
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sc}}(r,\mathcal{N})$
$\displaystyle=\lim_{n\to\infty}-\frac{1}{n}\log P_{\mathrm{s}}^{\star}(n,r;\mathcal{N}).$
(2)
It describes the optimal exponential decay of decoding success
at rates above the classical capacity.
Cheng and Tomamichel [CT26, Theorem 5]
proved that the limit exists for every  $r\geqslant 0$  and
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sc}}(r,\mathcal{N})$
$\displaystyle=\sup_{\alpha>1}\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\left[r-\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}(\mathcal{N}^{\otimes n})\right].$
(3)
Thus, determining the exponent reduces to removing the
regularization of the sandwiched Rényi Holevo information
$\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}$ , defined in Section 2.
In contrast to the entropy argument of [TZBW26],
this approach requires control at every order  $\alpha>1$ ,
not only in the limit  $\alpha\to 1^{+}$ .
Theorem 1 (Strong converse exponent).
For every  $\gamma,N\in[0,1]$ ,  $\alpha>1$ , and positive integer  $n$ ,
$\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}^{\otimes n})$
$\displaystyle=n\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}).$
(4)
For every  $r\geqslant 0$ , the limit in (2)
exists and satisfies
$\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{sc}}(r,{\cal A}_{\gamma,N})$
$\displaystyle=\sup_{\alpha>1}\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}[r-\widetilde{\chi}_{\alpha}({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})].$
(5)
Taking  $\alpha\to 1^{+}$  in (4) gives
the following capacity formula.
Corollary 2 (Classical capacity).
For every  $\gamma,N\in[0,1]$ ,
$\displaystyle C({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})$
$\displaystyle=\chi({\cal A}_{\gamma,N}).$
(6)
The main task is to establish (4). We follow the norm-based approach of Wilde, Winter, and
Yang [WWY14], which relates the sandwiched
Rényi information radius to maximum output norms of sandwiched maps.
Our main technical result establishes the required multiplicativity
for GADCs sandwiched by arbitrary nonnegative diagonal operators
(Theorem 4).
Phase covariance makes these diagonal operators sufficient for
the reference-state optimization.
The construction decomposes the joint output into a convex combination
of two positive operators with triangular factors.
Replacing each block of these factors by its Schatten norm
produces scalar matrices with identical Gram matrices.
A sharp triangular norm-compression inequality bounds each term
by the same one-copy output norm.

3 Additivity of Holevo Rényi information
We prove the additivity statement in
Theorem 1 through three steps.
First, we establish a Schatten-norm compression inequality
for triangular block matrices.
We then apply it to prove multiplicativity of the maximum output norm
for diagonally sandwiched GADCs.
Finally, phase covariance and the norm
representation (21) convert this multiplicativity
into additivity of Holevo Rényi information,
following the framework of [WWY14].
3.1 Schatten-norm compression
We first establish the triangular norm-compression inequality
used to control the factors in the output decomposition.
Theorem 3 (Schatten-norm compression).
For every  $2\leqslant p\leqslant\infty$  and rectangular matrices  $U,V,W$
of compatible sizes,
$\displaystyle\left\|\begin{pmatrix}U&0\\
V&W\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{p}$
$\displaystyle\leqslant\left\|\begin{pmatrix}\|U\|_{p}&0\\
\|V\|_{p}&\|W\|_{p}\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{p}.$
(23)
The constant one is sharp for every prescribed triple of nonnegative
block norms and every compatible choice of positive block dimensions.
The main step is to establish the previously missing range  $2<p<4$ .
Polar decomposition reduces the norm comparison to an inequality
for a trace-power difference.
Joint convexity allows us to remove off-diagonal entries from two
of its arguments; Jensen’s and Hölder’s inequalities then give
the scalar comparison.
The convexity argument extends the log-determinant method
of [TZBW26, Appendix A] from entropy to trace powers.
For  $p\geqslant 4$ , the result follows from Audenaert’s two-row
compression inequality [Aud08, Section 4.4],
based on King’s positive-block inequality [Kin03].
Proof.
Consider first square blocks of the same size and  $2<p<4$ .
Set  $s=p/2$  and  $T=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}U&0\\
V&W\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ .
Step 1: Gram-matrix reduction.
For positive semidefinite  $P,Q,R$  of a common dimension  $d$ ,
define the positive semidefinite block matrix
$\displaystyle Z(P,Q,R)$
$\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}P+Q&\sqrt{Q}\sqrt{R}\\
\sqrt{R}\sqrt{Q}&R\end{pmatrix}.$
(24)
Choose polar decompositions  $V=U_{V}\sqrt{V^{\dagger}V}$  and
$W=U_{W}\sqrt{W^{\dagger}W}$ , extending the polar factors to unitaries.
With  $J=U_{V}^{\dagger}U_{W}$ , set
$P=U^{\dagger}U$ ,  $Q=V^{\dagger}V$ , and  $R=JW^{\dagger}WJ^{\dagger}$ .
Then
$\displaystyle(I\oplus J)T^{\dagger}T(I\oplus J^{\dagger})$
$\displaystyle=Z(P,Q,R).$
(25)
To compare the block matrix with its scalar compression,
define the trace-power difference
$\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R)$
$\displaystyle=\operatorname{Tr}P^{s}+\operatorname{Tr}Q^{s}+\operatorname{Tr}R^{s}-\operatorname{Tr}Z(P,Q,R)^{s}.$
(26)
We use the same notation for nonnegative scalar arguments;
the scalar function is homogeneous of degree  $s$ .
The desired norm comparison reduces to
$\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R)$
$\displaystyle\geqslant F_{s}(\|P\|_{s},\|Q\|_{s},\|R\|_{s}).$
(27)
Indeed, replacing  $P,Q,R$  by their Schatten  $s$ -norms preserves
the first three terms of  $F_{s}$ .
Thus, a lower bound on  $F_{s}$  gives an upper bound on
the Schatten  $s$ -norm of the Gram matrix.
The identities  $\|P\|_{s}=\|U\|_{p}^{2}$ ,  $\|Q\|_{s}=\|V\|_{p}^{2}$ ,
and  $\|R\|_{s}=\|W\|_{p}^{2}$  identify the required scalar comparison.
Step 2: Scalar compression.
First suppose  $Q>0$ , and choose an eigenbasis with eigenvalues  $q_{i}$ .
Let  $x_{i},z_{i}$  be the diagonal entries of  $P,R$  in this basis,
and set  $y=\|Q\|_{s}$ .
We have
$\displaystyle F_{s}(P,Q,R)$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(a)}}{\geqslant}\sum_{i}F_{s}(x_{i},q_{i},z_{i})$
$\displaystyle=y^{s}\sum_{i}\frac{q_{i}^{s}}{y^{s}}F_{s}\!\left(\frac{x_{i}}{q_{i}},1,\frac{z_{i}}{q_{i}}\right)$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(b)}}{\geqslant}y^{s}F_{s}\!\left(\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(Q^{s-1}P)}{y^{s}},1,\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(Q^{s-1}R)}{y^{s}}\right)$
$\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{(c)}}{\geqslant}y^{s}F_{s}\!\left(\frac{\|P\|_{s}}{y},1,\frac{\|R\|_{s}}{y}\right)$
$\displaystyle=F_{s}(\|P\|_{s},\|Q\|_{s},\|R\|_{s}).$
(28)
For step (a), average simultaneous conjugations of  $P,Q,R$
by diagonal sign unitaries in the chosen eigenbasis of  $Q$ .
This fixes  $Q$  and removes the off-diagonal entries of  $P,R$ .
The resulting Gram matrix is a direct sum of scalar  $2\times 2$  blocks.
Unitary invariance and joint convexity in  $(P,R)$ ,
proved in Lemma 5
(Appendix A), give the inequality.
The next equality uses homogeneity, and step (b) applies
Jensen’s inequality with weights  $q_{i}^{s}/y^{s}$ , which sum to one.
For step (c), Hölder’s inequality gives
$\operatorname{Tr}(Q^{s-1}P)\leqslant y^{s-1}\|P\|_{s}$  and similarly for  $R$ .
Scalar monotonicity from the same lemma gives the inequality
in the stated direction.
The final equality again uses homogeneity.
Continuity, with  $Q$  replaced by  $Q+\epsilon I$ ,
extends (27) to  $Q\geqslant 0$ .
Write  $a=\|U\|_{p}$ ,  $b=\|V\|_{p}$ , and  $c=\|W\|_{p}$ .
Combining the two steps yields
$\displaystyle\|T\|_{p}^{2}$
$\displaystyle=\|Z(P,Q,R)\|_{s}\leqslant\left\|\begin{pmatrix}a^{2}+b^{2}&bc\\
bc&c^{2}\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{s}=\left\|\begin{pmatrix}a&0\\
b&c\end{pmatrix}\right\|_{p}^{2}.$
(29)
This proves the claimed inequality throughout  $2<p<4$ .
For  $4\leqslant p<\infty$ , it is the triangular specialization
of [Aud08, Section 4.4]; at  $p=2$ , it is the Frobenius identity.
Zero padding embeds compatible rectangular blocks into square blocks
of a common size, preserving the nonzero singular values of every
block and of the full matrix.
The limit  $p\to\infty$  gives the operator-norm endpoint.
Finally, choose unit vectors  $|u_{1}\rangle,|u_{2}\rangle,|v_{1}\rangle,|v_{2}\rangle$
in the corresponding row and column spaces, and set
$U=a|u_{1}\rangle\!\langle v_{1}|$ ,  $V=b|u_{2}\rangle\!\langle v_{1}|$ ,
and  $W=c|u_{2}\rangle\!\langle v_{2}|$ .
The full matrix is then an isometric embedding of its scalar compression,
proving sharpness for every  $a,b,c\geqslant 0$ .
∎
3.2 Multiplicativity of maximum output norm
The compression inequality now yields multiplicativity of the maximum
output norm for the GADC sandwiched by any nonnegative diagonal operator.
Theorem 4 (Sandwiched norm multiplicativity).
For every  $\gamma,N\in[0,1]$ , every nonnegative diagonal  $H$ ,
every finite-dimensional completely positive map  $\Phi$ ,
and every  $1\leqslant p\leqslant\infty$ ,
$\displaystyle\nu_{p}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H}\otimes\Phi)$
$\displaystyle=\nu_{p}(({\cal A}_{\gamma,N})_{H})\nu_{p}(\Phi).$
(30)
The input and output dimensions of  $\Phi$  are arbitrary,
and neither map is required to preserve trace.
The proof decomposes the joint output into a convex combination
of two positive operators with triangular factors.
The decomposition parameter is chosen from the block norms so that
both factors have the same scalar Gram matrix after compression.
Theorem 3 and the triangle inequality then
reduce the joint output norm to a one-copy output norm
times a scalar controlled by  $\nu_{p}(\Phi)$ .
Proof.
First assume  $1\leqslant p<\infty$  and  $0<\gamma,N<1$ .
Convexity of the Schatten norm reduces the optimization to
normalized pure inputs
$|\psi\rangle=|0\rangle\otimes|u\rangle+|1\rangle\otimes|v\rangle$ ,
where  $\langle u|u\rangle+\langle v|v\rangle=1$ .
Since  $\Phi$  is completely positive, the intermediate output is
positive semidefinite and admits the factorization
$\displaystyle R$
$\displaystyle:=(\operatorname{id}\otimes\Phi)(|\psi\rangle\!\langle\psi|)=\begin{pmatrix}\Phi(|u\rangle\!\langle u|)&\Phi(|u\rangle\!\langle v|)\\
\Phi(|v\rangle\!\langle u|)&\Phi(|v\rangle\!\langle v|)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}X\\
Y\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X^{\dagger}&Y^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}.$
(31)
Set  $m=\|X\|_{2p}^{2}+\|Y\|_{2p}^{2}$ .
If  $m=0$ , the output vanishes and the desired bound is immediate.
Otherwise, set  $q=\|Y\|_{2p}^{2}/m$  and first assume
that both  $X$  and  $Y$  are nonzero, so  $0<q<1$ .
Step 1: Decompose the output into triangular factors.
Write  $t=t_{\gamma,N}(q)$  and  $D=D_{\gamma,N}(q)$ .
The interior assumptions ensure  $0<t<1$  and  $D>0$ .

## 4. Selected route II: local energy, dressing, and positive constraints

### 4.1 Why the raw positive-bond comparison does not work

Each h_j has eigenvalues −2,−1,1, so k_j=h_j+2I≥0. Set K_0=H_L(1)+2LI. For |a_j−1|≤ε,

(1−ε)K_0≤Σ_j a_j k_j≤(1+ε)K_0.

The scalar shift −2Σ_j a_j does not change the perturbed gap. Min–max thus gives the lower bound

gap H_L(a)≥(1−ε)gap H_L(1)−2ε E_0(K_0).

HP's actual three-site energy inequality h_{12}+h_{23}≥−3I yields E_0(K_0)≥L/2. Thus the unremoved frustration energy is extensive. One cannot cancel the two occurrences of E_0(K_0) as if every local k_j annihilated Ω. For the special case a_j≡a the exact answer is a·gap H_L(1), illustrating that this comparison discards a real cancellation rather than disproving robustness.

Nor can one simply center every perturbing bond and bound it by the excitation energy. Here is an obstruction **inside the target's unperturbed Heisenberg family**, for every L divisible by four and L≥2304.

In Cartesian coordinates let A=Σ_{i,j}|i i j j〉 and B=Σ_{i,j}|i j j i〉 on four sites. These are unnormalized products of two singlets. For the open four-site Hamiltonian, direct integer contraction gives

Gram(A,B)=[[9,3],[3,9]],
〈(A,B),H_open(A,B)〉=[[-36,-18],[-18,-18]].

The vector A+B/4 therefore has Rayleigh quotient −246/59<−4. Tiling the ring with normalized copies gives zero expectation on the joining bonds, because each block is a rotational singlet. Hence E_0(H_L)/L≤−123/118<−1. The unique periodic ground state's bond expectation e_L is the same at every site by translation invariance. It is strictly greater than −2: equality would put every neighboring pair in its one-dimensional singlet space, impossible on three sites. For example, a pure state with the first pair a singlet factors that pair from the rest, whereas a second overlapping pair cannot simultaneously be a pure singlet. Consequently −2<e_L<−1, and h_jΩ is not a scalar multiple of Ω, since those are consecutive bond eigenvalues.

For a fixed bond define W=h_j−e_L I, χ=WΩ≠0, and K=H_L−E_0. Then χ⊥Ω and, for ψ_t=Ω+tχ,

〈ψ_t,Wψ_t〉=2t||χ||²+t²〈χ,Wχ〉,
〈ψ_t,Kψ_t〉=t²〈χ,Kχ〉.

No finite C can make |〈ψ,Wψ〉|≤C〈ψ,Kψ〉 hold for all ψ. The linear term defeats the quadratic one as t→0. This is a rigorous obstruction to an **undressed** relative-form lemma, not to H: ordinary perturbation theory changes the ground vector precisely to remove this term. ## 6. Additional exact checks on the spectral screen

### Stationary large lags: a technical consequence

FU writes A_n(t)=∫e^{-tλ}dν_n(λ) with ν_n nonnegative, and proves A_g(t)→0 as t→∞. For each n, A_n is nonnegative and decreasing. Therefore, for any η>0,

lim_{T→∞} limsup_n P{sup_{t≥T}A_n(t)>η}=0.

Indeed the supremum is A_n(T); weak convergence at each fixed T and the Portmanteau bound reduce the limsup to P{A_g(T)≥η}, which tends to zero. Together with compact convergence, this yields stationary convergence in the uniform-on-[a,∞) topology for each a>0 (with vanishing-at-infinity functions). A usual truncation at T proves tightness and identifies the limit. This applies to both disorder laws. It uses the source's positivity/decay directly and does not pay the waiting-time requirement W.

### A reversible delayed-bump test

Here is an exact finite-state obstruction to the suggested inference “compact convergence plus relaxation of the limit plus bounded evolved densities implies W.” It does not satisfy all SK source hypotheses, and is not a counterexample to W.

On {−1,1}³ use independent reversible coordinate-flip chains for x,y,z, with decay eigenvalues 1/N,2/N,1. Thus their flip rates are half these values and the invariant law π is uniform. Start from density h_0=1+α(x−y), α=1/4, relative to π. It is a probability density in [1/2,3/2]. At time s,

h_s=1+αe^{-s/N}x−αe^{-2s/N}y,

so those same bounds hold for all s≥0. The observable f=z(1+x+y)/3 has |f|≤1 and πf=0. Direct product-semigroup calculation gives

A_N(t)=e^{-t}(1+e^{-t/N}+e^{-2t/N})/9,
B_N(s,t)−A_N(t)=αe^{-t}/9 · [(1+e^{-t/N})e^{-s/N}−(1+e^{-2t/N})e^{-2s/N}].

Both functions converge on compact positive-time sets to A(t)=B(s,t)=e^{-t}/3. The limiting quench is stationary and decays in lag. For every finite N the chain eventually relaxes. But at s=N log2 and any fixed t>0,

B_N(N log2,t)−A_N(t)→e^{-t}/72>0.

Consequently the desired supremum over late waiting times cannot be inferred from just those properties. The calculation is verified on the actual eight-state product kernels at 27 rational attenuation triples; it is not a free choice of arbitrary continuous functions. A low-energy compactness or uniform-relaxation input excluding such hidden modes is substantive. The Gaussian warming bound alone does not exclude this example: its finite state space even has a uniformly bounded kernel. This observation does not assess whether the **other** detailed edge estimates in QU can eventually supply the required missing input.

4. **The exact reconstruction threshold for the three-state symmetric channel**, `sections/03-positive.tex`: `pos:additive`, `pos:moment-bounds` and `pos:correlation-bound` concern a common limiting fixed-point law with dλ²=1. The coefficient α uses the regular or Poisson factorial moment. Section `04-local.tex`, `loc:pair` permits distinct pair messages, but `loc:gap` subsequently returns to a common fixed-point law. These are not an arbitrary-tree reconstruction criterion.
5. **Classical capacity and entropy inequalities for generalized amplitude damping**, `sections/partners.tex`, proof of `cor:partner-additivity`: all finite-dimensional CPTP partner channels are allowed. Entropy additivity is not by itself a Rényi estimate above order one.
6. **The entropy photon-number inequality**, `sections/00-introduction.tex`, `thm:epni`: independent input ports, arbitrary internal multimode entanglement, finite energy. It does not permit replacing ordinary entropies with conditional entropies of ports sharing quantum memory.

## A variable-edge necessary condition

This is a proved preliminary extension of the source's necessity argument, **not a substantial accepted finding**. Its derivation is close to the source proof, and independent review has not yet been commissioned.

Let T have at most B≥1 children per vertex. Associate to edge e=(v,w) a four-state symmetric ferromagnetic channel parameter 0<λ_e<1, with uniform root. Put

\[
 r_e=\lambda_e^2,\qquad R_\rho=1,\qquad
 R_w=\prod_{e\in[\rho,w]}r_e.
\]

For a nonnegative conserved flow θ to infinity, define

\[
 \mathcal V(\theta)=\sup_{\xi\in\partial T}
 \sum_{e=(v,w)\in\xi}(1-r_e^2)
       \left(\frac{\theta(e)}{R_w}\right)^2,
 \qquad
 \mathcal C(T)=\sup\{|\theta|:\mathcal V(\theta)\le1\}.
\]

**Necessary condition.** If level observations reconstruct the root, then C(T)>0. No uniform separation of λ_e from one or zero is assumed.

**Proof.** Let m_v be the limiting quadratic information about the spin at v from levels of its descendant subtree. Data processing gives the limit in [0,3]; reconstruction gives m_ρ>0. For the finitely many children w of v write b_w=r_(v,w)m_w, S=Σb_w and

\[
 D=\max_{w\ne w'}b_wb_{w'}(b_w+b_{w'}),
\]

with D=0 if fewer than two children exist. At finite depth, combine the maximizing pair first and use the accepted moment-saving inequality and Jensen. Combine other children by subadditivity and pass to the limit. This proves m_v≤S−cD. As in the source, S³≤Σb_w³+B³D: each mixed monomial is bounded by D and there are at most B³ ordered triples.

Choose K=c/B³ and let y_v=m_v+Km_v³. Then

\[
 y_v\le S-cD+KS^3\le S+K\sum_w b_w^3
 =\sum_w r_e y_w-K\sum_w r_e(1-r_e^2)m_w^3.
\]

Since y_w≤(1+9K)m_w, set a=2K/(1+9K)³ to obtain

\[
 y_v\le\sum_w r_e y_w
       \left(1-\frac a2(1-r_e^2)y_w^2\right)
 \le\sum_w\frac{r_e y_w}
                   {\sqrt{1+a(1-r_e^2)y_w^2}}.
\]

The last inequality follows from (1+2t)^(−1/2)≥1−t for t≥0. Select coefficients d_e between zero and the displayed coefficient r_e/√(1+a(1−r_e²)y_w²) so that y_v=Σd_e y_w; multiply all upper-bound coefficients by a common ratio when necessary. Set ℓ_ρ=1, ℓ_w=ℓ_vd_e, and θ(e)=ℓ_wy_w. This is a conserved flow of mass y_ρ. With g_v=ℓ_v/R_v,

\[
 a(1-r_e^2)\left(\frac{\theta(e)}{R_w}\right)^2
 \le g_v^2-g_w^2.
\]

Telescoping along each ray gives aV(θ)≤1. Thus √a θ is admissible for C(T) and has positive mass √a y_ρ. All finite subtrees use the preserved posterior-law class; the argument does not require membership of a limiting law in that class. ∎

### Why the weight matters: an exact ray example

On a single infinite ray let λ_n=1−1/(n+1)² for edge n≥1. The product through depth n is

\[
 P_n=\prod_{j=1}^n\lambda_j=\frac{n+2}{2(n+1)}\longrightarrow\frac12.
\]

Symmetric channels compose by multiplying their parameters. The posterior given the endpoint is therefore a four-state channel row with parameter P_n. Its total-variation distance from uniform is 3P_n/4, tending to 3/8. Reconstruction holds.

The naive replacement of λ^(−2 depth) by R_n^(−1)=P_n^(−2) in the *unweighted* capacity has zero capacity: every nonzero ray flow is constant, and ΣP_n^(−4) diverges. In contrast,

\[
 \sum_{j=1}^n(1-\lambda_j^4)P_j^{-4}
 =P_n^{-4}-1\longrightarrow15.
\]

The weighted capacity is exactly 1/√15 on this ray. The example invalidates the naive extension, without challenging any accepted fixed-channel theorem.

### Remaining substantive step

It is not established here that C(T)>0 is sufficient for reconstruction on every bounded-degree variable-channel tree. Copying the fixed-channel proof is insufficient: its third-moment constant and geometric path-kernel bound deteriorate as λ approaches one, and weighted capacity alone does not bound the unweighted sum of profile squares on a ray. A new estimate must respect the factors 1−λ_e⁴ or use an appropriate coarse-graining argument without silently losing the bounded-degree hypotheses. The ray example tests a proposed criterion; it does not prove its sufficiency.

## Two quantum-information exclusions

**Current prior art for amplitude damping.** [Kun Fang, arXiv:2609.14621v2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.14621v2), Theorem 1, states the exact strong-converse exponent for every damping and thermal parameter, using additive sandwiched Rényi Holevo information for all orders above one. The version history reports revision on 6 October 2026. Earlier indexed descriptions concerned only a capacity bound. The exact proposed extension is therefore already claimed with a full proof in this current primary manuscript; it is not pursued as a new result. This screen is not an independent audit of that external proof.

**Quantum-memory EPnI obstruction.** [De Palma–Trevisan, arXiv:1706.00440](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.00440), Theorem 7, gives Gaussian sequences conditionally independent over quantum memory that asymptotically attain the conditional entropy-power bound for prescribed input conditional entropies. Apply it at equal mixing, with limiting input entropies g(1) and g(3). The limiting output entropy power is

\[
 \tfrac12 e^{g(1)}+\tfrac12 e^{g(3)}
 =\tfrac12(4+256/27)=182/27.
\]

A conditional EPnI would instead require a limiting output entropy at least g(2), whose exponential is 27/4. The ratio is 729/728>1. By continuity, sufficiently late finite-energy states in that sequence violate the proposed conditional EPnI. Both input conditional entropies are positive eventually. This is a direct consequence of established optimality, not a new countable finding.
